{{0=Letter from Oliver - 2 March 1863. Romania.}}

As mariners are wont to say - there is always a lull before the storm. As I am wont to say - a lowering of barometric pressure generally occurs before the storm. And this idiom certainly applies to the horror of my current situation.

My family's manor is set on a small precipice, its imposing iron gate emerging from the forest like the mouth of an otherworldly beast. You have no doubt seen the daguerreotype, so I will not delve further into detail. I remembered the daunting architecture from my youth, and returning to claim my inheritance left me feeling trepidatious.

Whatever the cause, it appears the delirium of the past has ebbed and conversations about the darker history of the town are now relegated to whispers in private. The consensus is that justice has been served and modern living has prevailed over the old ways. In fact, there are many who deny that the events occurred at all.

The underlying symptoms of mass hysteria have channeled themselves into other menial and unproductive modes of thinking. I am of the opinion that they overcompensate for the shames of their past. While the ground has just been broken, the district has invested in the most modern alienist philosophies - absurd and untested as those theories are - and a new Asylum is being constructed to focus on the rehabilitation of the mind.

So, like a wolf licking its wounds, the town has returned to a relative peace. And for a moment, it seemed that the calm would provide a welcome atmosphere to return to my labors.

That is, until the Creature appeared in my window one night, its bulky frame wet with rain.
The Creature's Demands

Letter from {{0=Oliver}} - (Cont.)

To my surprise, the hideous monster could speak, his jaw supported by a crudely stitched black thread which exposed the inner muscle when it moved. In deep, guttural tones, he conveyed his hatred for my grandfather, who had created him and abandoned him, helpless in the wild. "I was forcefully orphaned. Left to fend for myself while his sons and daughters existed in luxury," he groaned.

They say the sins of the father are passed on to the children, but rarely does this obligation skip a full generation. "You owe me a great debt, and I am here to demand payment," he stated firmly, and obstructed my escape until he could finish his tale. I was awestruck by his chilling words and the revelation that our family's dark secrets were indeed a reality.

Cursed into existence despite his decaying form, my grandfather's experiment demanded to live out his days with a faithful companion, another being who can understand the torture of existence. That it was my family's duty to atone for these sins and create it for him!

With a final turn, his grotesque figure framed in moonlight, he vowed that if we did not, he would exact a terrible vengeance upon our houses, so that we may know first-hand what torment he has endured!

If it weren't enough to stunt my studies with niceties, the event that followed a few days later served to compound my annoyance with this pseudoscience. One of my servants had willingly admitted themselves to this untested facility! And after all the care I had given them!

Letter from {{0=Oliver}} - (cont.)

I have left out one singular detail of the event that gained my attention. As I was heading to my carriage, a tall old man with a long white mustache accosted me and noticed my disapproval of the situation. He was clad in black from head to foot with ruddy lips, frosted eyebrows, and a distinct paleness to his features.

While other institutions across Europe experienced the ravenous strain of overcrowding, our town's well-funded lunatic asylum proved a luminous model of rehabilitation. Restraints were traded for personal care from the staff and a work release program was expanded for patients eager to assimilate themselves into society once again, with the skills to succeed.

It is an interesting concept in theory, but one which we know will only end in folly. When I made a brief visit to the Asylum Program (as they now so boldly call it), they even attempted to evaluate me as if I had been admitted. Like mighty Atlas, I will accept these heavy charges. While I disagree with their methodology, and the expenses of this progressive approach will certainly be a financial burden, access to skilled labor does appeal to me from an efficiency standpoint, if they have the stomach for it.

The days are certainly bright here in the valley, but in the end, this light will only make my family's work shine more brilliantly!

Correspondence - {{0=winner}} - 25 June, 1926

It feels like ages since I have written. The village that we once sojourned to all those years ago has fallen silent. It's crumbling defenses are a reminder - a metaphor for the crippling isolation of xenophobia. Even now I remember those accursed city walls that sapped my youthful vitality with every visit into the murky depths of that place - a place that could never be rebuilt after the hideous Experiment was unleashed.

Yet, even now the indomitable pull of my family's infamous work tears at my very soul! No. I cannot carry on a legacy of fear that left an entire town and estate in ruins. My colleagues at the university have no reverence for me. They laugh so heartily when I tell them the town in which I was birthed. I do not blame them. My hope is that I shall never see that foul place again. How could my family cultivate such an embarrassing line of thinking?

As I pen this note, my lawyer has made arrangements for a transfer of ownership - the deed to that wretched estate will soon finally be wrested from my hands and with it, the insidious efforts contained within will be buried forever.


THE END?

Springtime for {{0=town name}}

Correspondence from {{0=winner}} - 14 June, 1925

If you can smell the scent of tea and rich pastries on this paper before you, it is because I write this letter to you from one of my favorite shops along the main street. The shuffling footsteps and metal din of automobiles along concrete allows my thoughts to wander. I find it disagreeably bright in these parts nowadays, but at least they serve a damn fine cuppa. There are definite benefits to traveling merchants offering a steady supply of fine goods.

It appears we have emerged from the dismal environs of yesteryear into a full springtime bloom. My family may have made a few missteps, but it seems their kind-hearted souls (of which I was not aware) won the day and assuaged the fears of the populace. I will say that it is rather enjoyable to sketch out new scientific diagrams in broad daylight without scrutiny.

There are even some willing to volunteer their time towards my "eccentric hobbies" as they call them. Such insufferable fools. I will take pleasure in exploiting their ignorance. But, I will try to be sensible about it - it is unseasonable weather for painful howling.

Anyway, send my best wishes to your mother and do not tarry too long.

Yours Always,


THE END?
The Anger of the Mob

Letter from {{0=winner}} - 4 January, 1924

It finally happened. They destroyed it all. Mobs with actual torches and pitchforks, I tell you, knocked down my properly erected fencing and stormed the estate, destroying my parents' work. The curs had the audacity to arrive unannounced - had I not heard the hounds eviscerating several members of the crowd, I may not have escaped before being swallowed up by the flames.

The grounds still remain fallow and singed by ash, enveloping the plot in a vast, dreary grayness. My entreaties to the governor have been met with indifference and ridicule. It is clear that I will receive no financial remuneration for this riotous behavior. Am I to be forever punished for the sins of my father?

No matter! What do they know of loss? I have lost everything. My family's legacy is in tatters. They drive us away as if we are the outsiders, like foreign beggars.

This is not over. I will have vengeance. This paltry village will rue the day it crossed the Fourth of my line!


Also, if you would be so kind as to furnish me a small loan, it would certainly expedite my ability to obtain said revenge.


THE END?

Journal Entry - {{0=winner}} - 16 August, 1929

Sunday: I had the glorious dream again - it never fails to reinvigorate me, as I could relive that moment each night for the remainder of my years and be content.

I watch with steady eyes as my family's creation, {{1=champion name}}, with cathartic ambivalence, lifts the severed head of {{2=warden name}} high into the air. I feel the searing heat of burning oil, hear the hiss of rising steam and smoke, and smell the rusted iron in the air. The crowded arena cheered even as their leader was torn from his makeshift throne and tossed lifeless to the dusty Earth, blood pooling beneath, dark and thick as motor oil.

These images appear in my mind like light on silver even as my weathered hands strain to grasp the quill. My last act of defiance, perhaps. But what is the worth of toppling a regional tyrant? All this effort to shake the world, and barely one square kilometer has been rattled.

The inmates have moved on. The town is an empty, ruined field without vegetation - a decaying pile of ash, rust, and mud. Some days my mind feels the same. The sense of peace does nothing to stem this emptiness of purpose inside of me. {{3=?|An old man visits now and then - a friend of the family with a withered face that he keeps wrapped tightly with a scarf.}}

What a waste contentment is! What a terrible investment! I only hope my progeny will leave this broken land behind and forge a new path.


THE END?

Letter from {{0=letter author}} - 12 November, 1924.

It is my hope that this letter finds you well. The news I hear from Bucharest is positive, with a seasonable chill in the air and continued peace. As such, I pray you will indulge me in forgoing pleasantries and moving to matters of business with haste.

The institution in {{1=town name}} has been an unrivaled success. A steady stream of those suffering from insanities and delusions have been shipped here from other parts of the country. Yet still officials always wonder how we run such an efficient operation even as funding remains remarkably low. I believe it is in part due to the {{2=program name}} Program which has gained notoriety across Europe for its aggressive tactics. Those involved in the studies have shown a tremendous improvement in behavior.

Which is why I must repeat my strong request from my previous letter: we require more fresh patients to treat. Our near one hundred percent release rate has left several vacancies in the facility and we are in dire need to obtain more.

The concerns you expressed in your last letter are valid. What is the status of the released patients? How are we tracking their progress in society? How do you know we haven't simply been failing to treat them and then disposing of their bodies? Why are there bloodstains on the envelope of my previous letter? These are all important questions.

But, I ask you now - why question results?


THE END?
